title: vulkan: clamp A prefetch to end_k in coopmat1 int8 matmul
body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

Fixes #29342

The coopmat1 int8 matmul (mul_mmq_cm1_funcs.glsl) clamps the B prefetch to end_k, but the A prefetch still loads ib + ks for every k step. When K is not a multiple of BK*BK_STEP (128), the last k stepp of a row loads blocks of the next row, and for the last row it loads past the end of the tensor.

These loads are multiplied by a zeroed B step, so they usually add 0. But 0 * inf = NaN: if the next row has a non-finite scale, a row that does not contain it becomes NaN. Past the end of the tensor the read is out of bounds; on RADV it returns 0, but robustBufferAccess is not enabled, so this is not guaranted.

The fix is the same clamp as the B side: a k step past end_k reloads the step's first block, which is finite.

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

Test: test_mul_mat_row_inf (Q8_0, m=64, n=32, k=160 and 2880). All values are positive and the last row of A has an inf scale in block 0, so the expected output has +inf in that row only. Without the fix, row m-2 is NaN on vulkan. With GGML_VK_DISABLE_COOPMAT=1 it passes on master, so it covers the cm1 path.

title: cuda: add TQ2_0 dequant + MMVQ support
body:
### What this does

Adds CUDA support for `GGML_TYPE_TQ2_0` (upstream ternary type 35, group 256):
a dequantize path plus the MMVQ dispatch, so ternary models (BitNet b1.58, BitCPM,
Falcon3-1.58bit, ...) can keep their weights on the GPU instead of falling back to
the CPU for every MUL_MAT.

Scope mirrors the minimal approach of #28769 (dequant + MMVQ only) rather than the
fuller #11183 (which also adds MMQ/MMA tiles). 6 files, 95 added lines, no deletions.

### Changes

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/dequantize.cuh` | `dequantize_tq2_0` |
| `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/convert.cu` | 6 dispatch cases (`to_fp16/fp32/bf16` x `cont`/`nc`) |
| `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/common.cuh` | `ggml_cuda_type_traits<GGML_TYPE_TQ2_0>` (`qk=QK_K, qr=1, qi=QK_K/32`) |
| `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu` | 1 `supports_op` whitelist entry |
| `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/vecdotq.cuh` | `VDR_TQ2_0_Q8_1_MMVQ`, `tq2_0_crumbs_to_int8`, `vec_dot_tq2_0_q8_1` |
| `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/mmvq.cu` | 3 dispatch cases |

**Layout note** (the only difference from Q2_0): Q2_0 packs 4 consecutive elements
per byte; TQ2_0 stores 4 bit planes of 32 bytes, so element `n` sits at byte
`32*(n/128) + n%32` with shift `2*((n%128)/32)`. Same 2-bit code table
({0,1,2,3} -> {-1,0,+1,+2}), one fp16 scale per 256 weights.

### Measurements (RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, CUDA 13.1, sm_120, base master 1623d8c)

`llama-bench -p 512 -n 128`:

| Model | Before (CPU fallback) | **After (this PR)** | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| BitCPM-CANN-3B (3.61 B) | 21.6 t/s | **216.1 t/s** | 10.0x |
| BitCPM-CANN-8B (8.19 B) | 15.0 | **137.7** | 9.2x |
| BitNet-b1.58-2B-4T (2.41 B) | 22.9 | **45.2** | 2.0x |

Prefill (`pp512`): 5406 / 2590 / 6116 t/s respectively.

(The BitNet number is limited by its small size, not the kernel; large ternary
models see ~10x since the CPU fallback dominated.)

### Correctness

- **PPL unchanged**: BitCPM-3B, `llama-perplexity` on the same corpus:
  **6.4719 (this PR, GPU)** vs 6.4769 (CPU path) vs 6.4723 (PQ2_0 re-pack
  reference) - all three paths agree within noise.
- **Generation**: `llama-cli` greedy output is coherent and correct.
- **Unit check**: `tq2_0_crumbs_to_int8`'s `__byte_perm` lookup validated against
  a scalar reference on 20,000 random inputs (bit-exact).

### A pitfall worth flagging for reviewers

My first working version **passed PPL but produced garbage output**. Cause: the
decode path (MMVQ) and the prefill/dequant path use different kernels - the
`__byte_perm` selector in `tq2_0_crumbs_to_int8` was wrong (`x >> 8` instead of
`x >> 16`), which corrupted only the MMVQ path. Both paths must be tested end to
end; PPL alone is not sufficient. A repo-side op test for TQ2_0 MMVQ would catch
this class of bug - worth adding together with this change.

### Notes

- No MMQ/MMA tile path in this PR (mirrors #28769's scope). Happy to port the MMQ
  pieces from #11183 on top if maintainers want them.
- Rebased onto current master `1623d8c`; builds clean with CUDA 13.1 and no
  modifications outside the 6 files listed.
- Related: #11183 (stalled), issue #29058 (open).

title: test-llama-archs : toggle causal_attn to catch graph shape changes
body:
## Overview

This PR adds a check to `test-llama-archs` that the graph shape does not depend on `causal_attn`.

#28751 stopped re-reserving the scheduler when `causal_attn` changes, which is only safe if no model's graph shape depends on the flag. Until this PR, CI only toggled `causal_attn` through the server's tinygemma3 image tests, so this PR adds the check for every arch `test-llama-archs` covers.

After each row's existing decode, the check sets `causal_attn` off and decodes `n_ubatch/2` and then `n_ubatch` tokens. If the graph changes with the flag, the first decode re-plans the compute buffers for the smaller batch (the graph size changed, so this re-plan counts as expected, with `unexpected = false`). The second decode of `n_ubatch` tokens has the same graph shape as the first but larger tensors, so it needs a reallocation. This time the graph hasn't changed from the previous decode, so the re-plan is `unexpected = true` and aborts under `GGML_SCHED_NO_REALLOC`.

Since #28751, every arch the test covers passes.

title: RDNA3/4 Vulkan Large-Tile Split-K Optimization
body:
## Overview: RDNA3/4 Vulkan Large-Tile Split-K Optimization

## Background and Approach

This work focused on optimizing and validating the split-K strategy for large-tile matrix multiplication in the Vulkan backend. For prefill using a 128×128 tile with ubatch=512, the number of workgroups is `W = ceil(M/128) × 4`. The original strategy only split K when W did not exceed two-thirds of the CU count, which left some common matrices with underutilized tail rounds. For example, the AMD 7900 XTX has 96 CUs; M=4096 corresponds to 128 workgroups, so the second round only keeps 32 CUs busy.

The new strategy only kicks in on RDNA3/4 with large tiles when N≥512, K≥2048, and the original strategy would not split. It consists of two parts:

- **Cost model:** Based on the number of execution rounds, the K length of each segment, and the merge overhead, it compares not splitting, splitting into two, and splitting into three, then picks the option with the lowest estimated cost.
- **Direct rule:** When W falls between two-thirds and five-sixths of the CU count and K≥8192, split into three — provided the LDS capacity allows at least two workgroups to reside per CU.

Cases where the original strategy already splits, other architectures, small-to-medium tiles, and cases where W exceeds twice the CU count all remain unchanged.

## Theoretical Coverage

Whether a case is triggered depends on the relationship between tile count and CU count, not on the model name. The same matrix on a different device will lead to a different split decision.

| M, N=512 | Workgroups | R9700: 64 CU | 7900 XTX: 96 CU |
|---|---:|---|---|
| 1536 | 48 | May hit the direct rule with long K | Original strategy already splits in two, unchanged |
| 2560 | 80 | Second round only uses 16 CUs; cost model may trigger | Hits the direct rule with long K and sufficient resources |
| 3840 | 120 | Close to two full rounds; shapes in this test are not triggered | Second round only uses 24 CUs; cost model may trigger |
| 4096 | 128 | Both rounds fully packed, not triggered | Second round only uses 32 CUs; cost model may trigger |

Predicting from the dense matmul compute of the FP16 path, the triggered share on 64 CU for Gemma4 E4B and InternVL is about **34% and 29%** respectively; on 96 CU for Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 3 12B, and gemma-4-12b it is about **37%, 41%, and 40%** respectively. The measured split changes match these predictions.

## End-to-End Results

Testing covered seven models under FA enabled and ubatch=512, using three ABBA rounds with the first (warm-up) round discarded. Representative pp512 throughput improvements are shown below; pp1024 gains are close to these.

| GPU | Model | FP16 Path | INT8 MMQ Path |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| R9700 | Gemma4 E4B Q4_K_M | +7.1% | New strategy not triggered |
| R9700 | Gemma4 E4B Q4_0 | +6.1% | +4.3% |
| R9700 | InternVL3-2B Q8_0 | +4.2% | New strategy not triggered |
| 7900 XTX | Gemma 3 12B Q8_0 | +9.8% | +5.7% |
| 7900 XTX | gemma-4-12b Q4_0 | +9.8% | +6.4% |
| 7900 XTX | Qwen3.5-9B Q4_0 | +7.7% | +6.3% |

## Single-Operator Tests

The full local test set includes seven weight formats and 11 shapes. On the 7900 XTX, it passed 77/77 with MMQ enabled and 66/66 with it disabled. Two representative shapes are selected below, listing the measured timing for each format.

Conditions: N=512, input B in F32; timing is in **µs per run**, averaged over two runs per arm, with the improvement computed as `base / new - 1`. Quantized weights in the FP16 columns are dequantized to FP16 inside the shader before computation.

**Long K: M=3840, K=15360**

| Weight Format | FP16 base | FP16 new | Gain | INT8 base | INT8 new | Gain |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| F16 | 1615.2 | 1403.6 | +15.1% | N/A | N/A | N/A |
| Q4_0 | 1412.9 | 1075.2 | +31.4% | 1399.7 | 1115.4 | +25.5% |
| Q4_1 | 1379.3 | 1047.5 | +31.7% | 1469.4 | 1171.0 | +25.5% |
| Q8_0 | 1576.3 | 1196.6 | +31.7% | 1541.6 | 1170.0 | +31.8% |
| Q4_K | 1598.5 | 1297.3 | +23.2% | 1628.4 | 1320.5 | +23.3% |
| Q5_K | 1605.3 | 1266.9 | +26.7% | 1616.7 | 1330.2 | +21.5% |
| Q6_K | 1821.9 | 1451.2 | +25.5% | 1513.1 | 1524.0 | -0.7% |

**Shorter K: M=4096, K=4096**

| Weight Format | FP16 base | FP16 new | Gain | INT8 base | INT8 new | Gain |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| F16 | 406.1 | 356.1 | +14.0% | N/A | N/A | N/A |
| Q4_0 | 391.5 | 337.2 | +16.1% | 410.0 | 370.1 | +10.8% |
| Q4_1 | 393.1 | 333.5 | +17.9% | 441.0 | 384.8 | +14.6% |
| Q8_0 | 427.2 | 374.2 | +14.2% | 437.5 | 381.9 | +14.6% |
| Q4_K | 457.5 | 392.4 | +16.6% | 486.9 | 418.6 | +16.3% |
| Q5_K | 450.1 | 392.2 | +14.7% | 484.0 | 420.4 | +15.1% |
| Q6_K | 498.7 | 446.9 | +11.6% | 439.4 | 440.2 | -0.2% |

In both FP16 groups the decision changes from no split to splitting in three; INT8 also splits in three except for Q6_K. The Q6_K INT8 pipeline uses a 64×128 tile and does not enter the new strategy, serving as a control.

## Analysis and Trade-offs

The single-operator gains align with the end-to-end gains in direction, but the whole-model improvement also depends on the share of triggered operators. The FP16 pipeline uses about 12–21 KiB of LDS per workgroup, while the INT8 large tile uses about 40–44 KiB. For the latter, LDS capacity allows fewer resident workgroups per CU, so there is less room to increase concurrency.

I'd like us to discuss whether this strategy should cover only the **FP16 matmul path, including FP16 computation after dequantizing quantized weights**. Covering FP16 alone yields larger representative end-to-end gains and reduces pipeline resource bookkeeping and gating logic; this PR currently also covers INT8. The final decision needs to balance the breadth of the gains against implementation complexity.

title: quantize: add IQ2_NL and IQ3_NL types (CPU)
body:
## Overview

K-quants and I-quants operate on 256-element super-blocks. A tensor can use them only if its row length (`ncols`) is an exact multiple of 256. When it isn't, the quantizer falls back to a different (usually sub-optimal) 32-element block type per tensor.

Mainline 32-block types stop at 4.50 bpw (Q4_0/IQ4_NL) creating a hard floor on every misaligned tensor and therefore on the whole file wherever misaligned tensors dominate because there is nothing better to substitute to.

This PR introduces two new CPU-only types IQ2_NL (2.50 bpw) and IQ3_NL (3.50 bpw) extending the existing non-linear family downward. Being 32-block types, they apply wherever `ncols % 32 == 0`.

## Additional information

Test models and results including PPL, KLD and inference benchmarks available at [HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co/eaddario/IQ2_NL-IQ3_NL-Test-Models).

title: quantize: add option to automatically choose optimal quant types to reach a file/bpw target size at lowest error
body:
This PR adds `target_bpw_type()`, a function to determine an optimal per-tensor quantization mix to achieve a user-specified  total file size (i.e., `--target-size 1.5g`) or a global bits-per-weight (bpw) target (i.e., `--target-bpw 4.5678`).

The function solves a constrained optimization problem to minimize quantization error, subject to a global size budget. It estimates per-tensor error for each layer, and dynamically allocates the bit budget where it matters most.

### High level flow:
1.  **Error estimation via Monte Carlo sampling:** For every applicable tensor, the function computes the quantization error, dequantizing a subset of rows weighted by an importance matrix (imatrix).
2.  **Pareto Frontier analysis:** For each tensor, it identifies the [Pareto frontier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_front) discarding types that increase size without sufficiently decreasing error.
3.  **Lagrangian optimization:** It uses Lagrangian relaxation to find an optimal distribution of bits across the entire model. Higher bit-rates are dynamically allocated to tensors where they provide the highest reduction in error.
4.  **Resumable state:** When `--state-file` is set, target computations are saved to a file. If the quantization is interrupted (e.g., Ctrl+C), it can resume error calculation from where it left off in the next run.

### Advantages
1. **Target arbitrary size models**
    - The algorithm will produce a model (nearly) exactly of the requested file/bpw size, which is very useful for maximizing VRAM usage. In a system with 24GB VRAM and a 70B model, standard quants might produce a 16.8GB file (too small, quality left on table) or a 24.1GB file (won't fit). `--target-size 23.85g` will generate a 23.85 GiB file to utilize the hardware fully.

2. **Data-driven mixed precision often can improve quality at fixed size**
    - Instead of using hardcoded heuristics, that may be sub‑optimal for a given architecture or size, the mix is determined by the actual error sensitivity of the specific model's weights. This often yields a better quality/size trade-off, especially in aggressive quantization scenarios (1.5 to 3.5 bpw), or for unusual architectures.

3. **Allows better like-for-like comparisons between models and families**
    - Standard quantization uses hardcoded rules like: *"use Q4_K_M, except bump some tensors up/down, except fall back if incompatible, except keep some tensors unquantized..."* and consquently, two different models quantized at the same Q4_K_M level can end up with very different bpw (e.g. 4.75 and 4.30).

    - Model performance generally scales with size; larger models typically outperform smaller ones. A model quantized with more bits will usually perform better (exhibiting lower perplexity and better evaluation scores) than a smaller version, even when the same underlying quantization method is used. This makes performance comparisons between models not a controlled experiment, as the models being compared have different effective compression ratios.

    - `--target-bpw` helps to normalize experiments by forcing models to be quantized to a roughly equal overall byte budget. This standardization allows performance variations between models to be more accurately linked to underlying factors such as architectural or training differences, the effect of quantization error at the same compression level, or the decisions made by the optimizer regarding allocation.

### Disadvantages
1. **Quantization process is significantly slower than standard**
    - This approach can take 5x-10x longer as it quantizes a sample of most tensors into 15 different formats, dequantizes them back, computes error diffs, and selects the best size/error option that fits the target file size or global bpw budget.

    - However, the `--state-file` option will save the above-mentioned computations to disk so that future quantizations can be generated at normal speed. It also allows to interrupt the computation process and resume it at a later time.

2. **The optimization target is only a proxy for the model's performance quality**
    - The process minimizes a per-tensor estimated error computed from sampled rows, not actual perplexity or divergence of output distributions. Since errors interact nonlinearly across layers, there are no guarantees it will select the best possible mix subject to the file/bpw size constraint.

3. **An imatrix with activations data is required for best results**
    - The algorithm requires an imatrix generated by a yet to be merged pull request #14891 
    - Activation and statistics data are needed to compute the error. If the imatrix file does not contain the necessary data, `--target-bpw` and `--target-file` will refuse to run.

### Design considerations
The `target_bpw_type()` function is implemented as a container for several lambdas providing all the logic for serialization, multithreading, math/stats, and optimization.

Although there are clear downsides to this approach (i.e. cognitive load, testability and maintainability), a self-contained "God function" seemed a better choice to prevent `llama-quantize`'s global scope pollution: structs and helper lambdas are highly specific to this exact algorithm and have no reuse value elsewhere in the library.

Based on 88 tests with models from 22 different families, the `target_bpw_type()` optimization routine generated **~75%** better quality models as standard quantization.

title: [SYCL]: fix memory errors in mul_mat, split buffer, host pool
body:
## Overview

- `ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat_sycl`: use the packed staging of F16 `src1` for non-
      contiguous (view/bcast) reads, the original tensors were not packed row-
      major with row stride of `ne10`, so the pointer strided out-of-bounds.
- `ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat` (multi-GPU): `dev[i].src0_dd` was set to `(char *)
      src0->data` for a contiguous split `src0`, but a split tensor’s `->data` is
      a dummy base that is never dereferenced. The rows live in
      `src0_extra->data_device[i]`. The non-quantized cross-device `src1` copy
      read from `src1_extra->data_device[ctx.device]`, which is null when `src1`
      is notsplit (null deref). Fixed to copy from `dev[ctx.device].src1_ddf`.
- split buffer (multi-GPU): size the stream vector by device, consumers index
      it by device id; use the per-device `src0` slice and the main device `src1`
      staging for cross-device copies
- pool_host: per-instance counter, size-checked reuse, no double caching
     (double free), free instead of leak when all slots are cached
- L0 device malloc: request the advertised 128 B alignment
- assert 32-bit-indexed kernel element counts fit in int (cpy, scale,
      sum, sum_rows, mean, argmax, diag_mask_inf, roll)
- assert 128 B alignment for the ESIMD 1024-bit load launchers
- get_max_size: query the buffer type device, not the current device
- dev2dev_memcpy: check the host staging `malloc`
- supports_op: GLU only for f32/f16, the fused kernels have no other
      instantiations (bf16 hit the assert and aborted)
- supports_op: conv_3d only for non-degenerate shapes, k == 0 / m == 0
      made MKL sgemm throw (illegal lda) and abort
- supports_op: scale only for f32, the kernel is f32 only

## Additional information

**N.B.** Multiple GPU fixes are **not** tested on multiple GPU setup, as I don't have access to such. But have been tested on single GPU.

More details in #29888

title: model : add BerryLM support
body:
## Overview

This PR adds support for the BerryLM architecture (BerryLMForCausalLM, HF repo rwb-ai/BerryLM-OS) to llama.cpp.

BerryLM is an 18.29B-parameter hybrid MoE model with 3.19B active parameters per token. It has 40 layers: 30 KDA linear-attention layers and 10 gated full-attention layers inserted every 4th layer. The full-attention layers use 16 Q heads, 2 KV heads (GQA), head_dim=256, sigmoid output gate, QK RMSNorm, and partial RoPE over 25% of dimensions (64 of 256), with rope_theta=1e7. The KDA layers use 16 K heads, 32 V heads, head_dim=128, short conv kernel 4, per-channel forget gate via low-rank projection (rank 128), beta gate, and gated output RMSNorm.

The MoE block uses 128 routed experts with top-8 softmax routing and normalized top-k, expert FFN size 512, plus 1 shared expert (FFN 512) with a sigmoid gate. The residual stream uses Gated Block AttnRes with block size 8. Norms are RMSNorm with eps=1e-6. Vocab is 180224 BPE with tokenizer.ggml.pre = "berrylm". max_position_embeddings is declared as 262144; validation in this PR uses shorter contexts.

Implementation notes:

* No new ggml ops or backend code are introduced.

* KDA uses the shared delta-net base and generic ops only.

* Conversion-time transforms: (1 + w) norm weights folded; tanh of AttnRes gate folded; V heads reordered to ggml broadcast layout; fused expert gate_up split; ssm_f_a/ssm_f_b kept F32.

* Embeddings are untied.

body:
## Overview

In Firefox on http://localhost, navigator.clipboard.writeText exists, so the if condition is true. However, when it executes, Firefox throws a DOMException (because it's not a secure HTTPS context or transient focus was lost). Because it throws, execution immediately jumps to the catch block at the bottom, completely bypassing the execCommand fallback that was sitting right below it. 

The fallback is dead code. The Fix:

1) It attempts the modern API.

2) If Firefox throws an error, it is caught locally, logged as a warning, and the function continues to the next block. The next block uses document.execCommand('copy'), which is synchronous and much more lenient with Firefox's user-gesture requirements, successfully writing to the clipboard. title: ggml : speed up batch-1 CPU decode, align large allocations
body:
## Overview


Bbatch-1 decode attention process KV one position at a time. It uses scalar expf per position, rescales accumulator when new max is fund and converts Q to F16 then widens back (x86). The loop-carried max/rescale is serialized back.
Tiled path can't be uilized. because it requires GGML_FA_TILE_Q query rows, but decode only has one.

This PR: vlocks the KV loop, rescaling once every 32 elements. Keeps Q in F32 where K is F16, and mixed F16xF32 dor exists. 
Computes four K.Q dot products per Q load and accumulates V in F32 where a mixed multiply-add is used.
For Linux only: aligns allocations >=r 4MiB to 2MiB + madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE), retrying at ordinary alignment on failure.
Also the fallback is implemented when tiling is not feasible (quantized K/V, mismatched K/V types, DV not a multiple of the vector width, 2..63 query rows); this is not evaluated in the measurements.

## Additional information

Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M, tg at 8192-token context, THP madvise:

- Ryzen 7 9700X  +15.29%   (attention change alone +10.67%)
- Neoverse-N1    +9.22%    (attention change alone  +7.43%)

title: server : add logit_gate to /v1/completions and /v1/chat/completions
body:
## Overview

Add a `logit_gate` option to `/v1/completions` and `/v1/chat/completions`.
It runs one prefill and returns a probability distribution over a candidate
token set — no decoding, no sampling change.

How it works:
- One prefill only. Zero autoregression.
- Softmax over the candidate set on the last prompt token's logits.
- Returns one probability per candidate. It does not block or force tokens.

Two modes:
- `gate_only` (default): always return the distribution and stop.
- `gate_then_chat`: if the top probability is below the threshold, the gate
  misses and the same request continues as normal generation. Prefill is
  already paid, so nothing is wasted. `threshold` applies only to this mode.

Minimal request:

{"model": "qwen3", "prompt": "The capital of France is", "logit_gate": {"candidates": [{"label": "Paris", "text": " Paris"}, {"label": "Lyon", "ids": [43, 24198]}], "mode": "gate_only", "threshold": 0.9}}

`candidates` takes `ids`, or a `text` that tokenizes to exactly one token.
`ids` are tokenizer-specific.

Minimal response (gate_only, default):

{"choices": [{"text": "", "index": 0, "finish_reason": "stop"}], "logit_gate": {"best": "Paris", "prob": 0.9999, "fired": true, "threshold": 0.9, "confidence": 0.9988, "temperature": 1.0, "distribution": [{"label": "Paris", "prob": 0.9999}, {"label": "Lyon", "prob": 0.0001}]}}

Empty text + `finish_reason: stop` is what zero autoregression looks like.

Minimal response (gate_then_chat, below threshold): a plain completion, no
`logit_gate` field.

{"choices": [{"text": "Paris", "index": 0, "finish_reason": "stop"}]}

## Additional information

- See #29022
- Did not reuse `logit_bias`, because it only shifts logits; it cannot return a distribution or skip decoding.
- Out of scope: multi-token candidates must pass explicit `ids` (automatic prefix matching / Trie not done).
- Tests: tools/server/tests/unit/test_logit_gate.py

title: embeddings: skip logits and lm head during inference
body:
## Overview

This PR adds the no-logits mode which is an optional optimization for embedding workloads. When a causal model is used only for embeddings, the request needs the hidden states and pooled embeddings, but the regular path may still run the vocabulary projection and copy the unused logits to host memory. Enabling this mode skips that extra work while leaving the embedding calculation itself unchanged.

## Additional information

- `llama_context_params` now includes a public `no_logits_for_embeddings` option, which is disabled by default.
- The option is available through `--no-logits-for-embeddings` and `LLAMA_ARG_NO_LOGITS_FOR_EMBEDDINGS`.
- The logits path is bypassed only for embedding requests that enable this option, use `LLAMA_CONTEXT_TYPE_DEFAULT`, and do not configure a backend sampler.
- In that case, the computation graph is built from the embedding tensor rather than the logits tensor, leaving the vocabulary projection or LM head out of the graph.
- Because no logits output is needed, the runtime also skips allocating and copying the host-side raw-logits buffer. On this path, `llama_get_logits()` and `llama_get_logits_ith()` return `NULL`.
- Token-level and pooled embeddings continue to follow the same computation path as before.
- Existing behavior is retained when the option is disabled, as well as for generation, non-embedding requests, and requests that use a backend sampler.
- Graph-cache compatibility checks also take this option into account, so graphs with different output behavior are kept separate.

For example, a Qwen3 embedding request using LAST pooling would normally compute the hidden states and then run the LM head to produce a `[tokens, vocabulary]` logits tensor, even though those logits are not used afterward. With `--no-logits-for-embeddings` enabled, the graph ends at the embedding output instead. LAST pooling still uses the same embedding result, while the LM-head computation and host-side logits buffer are left out.

The tests cover the option from the CLI through to the runtime context. For Llama and Qwen3, they compare the enabled and disabled paths and expect both per-token and pooled embeddings to match exactly. There is also coverage for BERT and Llama Embed models, which do not have an LM head. Additional cases check that eligible embedding requests leave out the LM-head/logits branch, while text-generation and backend-sampler requests continue to produce logits.

## Overview

This has been on my todo list for a while: Overhaul the Vulkan backend host-visible memory management to allow multiple devices to access host memory. On master only the first device can directly read from host memory, which increases load times in multi-gpu systems and may make transfers slower.

This branch changes it to use `VK_EXT_external_memory_host` to use a regular aligned CPU allocation and access it from all devices. In my tests it reduces non-mmap multi-GPU load times by around 20%. No effect on inference performance.

Single-GPU systems should be unaffected.

title: mtmd : lfm2 tiles and layout match transformers
body:
## Overview

LFM2-VL, LFM2.5-VL, d1-3B and d1-omni cut a large image into 512x512 tiles plus a small thumbnail. llama.cpp did this differently from the reference Python code (transformers `Lfm2VlImageProcessor`, d1-omni's `vision.py`) in two ways:

- Tiles: Python stretches the image to fill the tile grid. llama.cpp kept the image's shape and filled the rest with black bars. This PR stretches for all LFM2 models, as llama.cpp already does for d1-omni (#30114).
- Layout: Python rounds halves to even and uses double precision when it picks the tile grid and the thumbnail size. llama.cpp used `std::round` and float, so 31,926 of the 16.8M image sizes up to 4096x4096 got another grid or thumbnail, and another number of tokens. For example, a 720x1600 image got 2x5 tiles instead of 2x4. This PR rounds as Python does, like #27057 already did for `should_tile`.

Only LFM2 code changes; other models are not affected.

## Additional information

Reproduction (prompt tokens: master 2812, this PR 2298, transformers 2298):

```sh
python3 -c "from PIL import Image; Image.new('RGB', (720, 1600), 'gray').save('img.png')"
llama-server -hf LiquidAI/LFM2.5-VL-450M-GGUF:F16 --port 8080 &
until curl -sf localhost:8080/health > /dev/null; do sleep 1; done
echo '{"max_tokens": 1, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "data:image/png;base64,'$(base64 < img.png | tr -d '\n')'"}}]}]}' > req.json
curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @req.json | jq .usage.prompt_tokens
python3 -c "from PIL import Image; from transformers import AutoProcessor; p = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained('LiquidAI/LFM2.5-VL-450M'); t = p.apply_chat_template([{'role': 'user', 'content': [{'type': 'image'}]}], add_generation_prompt=True); print(len(p(images=[Image.open('img.png')], text=t)['input_ids'][0]))"
```

With a 400x600 image: master 258, this PR 239, transformers 239.

Accuracy: the largest probability difference to the Python reference (fp32; d1: over the answer options, LFM2-VL: over transformers' top-20 next tokens), and the number of items with another prompt length. Master 50e3e3e48, Apple M3 Ultra (Metal), F16 models:

| model, test set | master | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| LFM2.5-VL-450M, 52 images | 0.193, 14 | 0.014, 0 |
| LFM2-VL-450M, 52 images | 0.503, 14, 2 top-1 flips | 0.145, 0, 0 |
| d1-omni-600M, 96 image questions | 0.954, 42, 4 flipped answers | 0.010, 0, 0 |
| d1-3B, 96 image questions | 0.356, 36 | 0.029, 6 (see below) |
| d1-3B, 450 POPE questions | 0.056, 5 | 0.009, 0 |

- LFM2-VL-450M stays at 0.145 because its published mmproj has no `clip.vision.image_resize_algo`, so llama.cpp resizes it with bilinear while transformers uses bicubic. With the key set to bicubic: 0.444 -> 0.003.
- The new layout code gives the same result as the Python code for every image size up to 4096x4096. Where the layout changes, 27,834 sizes get fewer tokens (up to 2048 fewer) and 4,092 get more: most by under 100 tokens, 523 by 256 to 1024 tokens (shapes that sit exactly between two grids, where Python picks the bigger grid).
- One case gets worse for d1-3B: its own runner shrinks images above 1 megapixel before tiling (720x1600 becomes 686x1526, 2x5 tiles). Master matched that by accident; this PR gives 2x4, as transformers does for the full image. 6 test items change: 3 worse (largest 0.019 -> 0.029), 3 better. Adding the shrink step is out of scope.

Speed follows the number of tokens. Whole-request time, this PR vs master 50e3e3e48 (F16, `-np 1`), on an H100 GPU (CUDA) and a 30-core Xeon 8358 (CPU):

| image (prompt tokens, master -> this PR) | CUDA (LFM2.5-VL / d1-3B) | CPU (LFM2.5-VL / d1-3B) |
|---|---|---|
| 504x1120 (2817 -> 761) | -65.0% / -69.4% | -73.6% / -72.6% |
| 720x1600 (2817 -> 2303) | -16.6% / -17.3% | -16.3% / -17.8% |
| 640x480, 1024x768, 2000x1500, 3024x4032 (unchanged) | -2.8% to +0.8% | within noise |
| 1000x1200 (1797 -> 2568) | +29.9% / +36.4% | +43.0% / +42.9% |
| 560x960 (771 -> 1799) | +90.6% / +111% | +124% / +131% |

Stretching costs nothing: preparing a 1024x768 image takes 25.9 ms instead of 31.0 ms (LFM2.5-VL, CUDA build).

Tests: `test-mtmd-impl` gets 4 thumbnail-size cases and 4 grid cases with the values transformers gives; master's code fails 6 of the 13 checks. The stretch is a loader setting and has no unit test. For a 1024x768 image on LFM2.5-VL-450M, master's tiles differ from transformers in 97.5% of the pixel values (up to 255, the black bars); this PR's tiles are identical.

title: sycl : accelerate MXFP4 MoE with arithmetic decoding and weight reordering
body:
## Overview

**Results:**
Speeds up MXFP4 MoE inference in the SYCL backend:
- gpt-oss-20b: 55.84 → 106.64 tok/s (1.91×) decode, 5 repetitions
- gpt-oss-120b on two cards: 33.27 → 67.14 tok/s (2.02×) decode, 2 repetitions
- gpt-oss-120b prompt processing: 594.5 → 600.1 tok/s
- gpt-oss-20b (8 × 2048 tokens) perplexity: 14.5148 → 14.5129

**Changes:**
- Replaces table-based MXFP4 decoding with bit-identical 32-bit arithmetic, avoiding costly permute emulation.
- Adds lazy, per-expert weight reordering to enable aligned vector loads, with reorder-aware decode, multi-token, and prefill paths.
- Limits temporary reorder memory to 32 MiB and preserves the generic fallback for misaligned tensors.

## Additional information
This was tested and benchmarked on Intel Arc Pro B70 GPUs running Windows 11 and oneAPI 2026.0 and AMD EPYC 7402P, with flash attention enabled.  Gpt-oss-20b ran on one card and gpt-oss-120b on two cards.

All MXFP4 backend tests pass on both devices: MUL_MAT 39/39 and MUL_MAT_ID 74/74. gpt-oss-20b perplexity remains within noise of the baseline.

Arithmetic decoding is the prerequisite for the weight-reordering optimization. Other GPUs and Linux have not been tested.

Prior to this change, the SYCL backend never created reorder metadata for the MXFP4 tensors, so the existing MXFP4 MUL_MAT_ID tests never exercised a reordered kernel.

title: Multi-column on Intel XMX matrix engines refactored
body:
## Overview

Multi-column (2 to 80 activation columns) mul_mat_vec_q for reordered K-quant and Q8_0 weights on the Intel XMX matrix engines (int8 DPAS, ESIMD), for the SYCL backend. It targets speculative decoding verification (2 to 8 tokens per step) and short prompt batches (9 to 80 tokens). Three types also use it for a single column (Q2_K, Q3_K, Q8_0).


## Additional information

The existing multi-column dp4a kernels redo the weight unpack and the per-column scale arithmetic for every column, so the cost grows with the batch size (about 5 lane operations per dp4a per extra column). Profiling showed the step time for 4 tokens was 46% above 1 token on a Q6_K model, and much worse for Q3_K. Decode of one token is bandwidth bound, speculative
verification is not, so this gap is important.

Hardware and setup: Intel Arc Pro B70 (32 GB), Windows 10, oneAPI 2026.1 (icx), Level Zero driver
1.15.37858, SYCL backend with `GGML_SYCL_F16=ON`, graphs on. `llama-bench -ngl 99 -fa 1 -r 3`.
All models are Qwen3.8 27B variants (qwen35 architecture). "Before" is the same build with
`GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_XMX=0`. Values are tokens per second, `ppN` is a batch of N tokens, so the step
time is N / value.

| Model (GB) | tg1 | pp2 | pp4 | pp8 | pp16 | pp32 |
| Q8_0 (29.0) | 15.9 -> 18.0 | 30.6 -> 36.0 | 58.4 -> 70.7 | 108.8 -> 133 | 32.4 -> 241 | 64.3 -> 266 |
| Q6_K (22.4) | 22.8 -> 22.8 | 41 -> 44.6 | 63 -> 86 | 79 -> 159 | 45 -> 210 | n/a |
| Q4_K_S (16.4) | 26.5 -> 26.5 | 41.1 -> 48.4 | 67.7 -> 90 | 82.7 -> 131 | 50.3 -> 308 | 99 -> 354 |
| Q3_K_S (12.7) | 28.9 -> 33.1 | 27.2 -> 62 | 44.7 -> 115 | 66.6 -> 192 | 36.2 -> 243 | 71.7 -> 269 |
| Q2_K (10.8) | 33.4 -> 37.6 | 31.3 -> 69 | 50.8 -> 121 | 71.9 -> 169 | 46.6 -> 235 | 91.9 -> 266 |

End to end with speculative decoding (--spec-type draft-mtp, n-max 4, p-min 0.5, temperature 0.75, 5 prompts of 400 tokens, average tokens per second; the trim column also sets LLAMA_MTP_DRAFT_VOCAB=98304):

| Model | XMX off | XMX on | XMX on + trim |
| Q8_0 | 32.4 | 40.3 | 43.1 |
| Q4_K_S | 38.7 | 47.6 | 51.0 |
| Q3_K_S | 28.6 | 53.6 | 57.2 (63 in a later run) |
| Q2_K | 30.2 | 60.0 | 63.9 |
| Q6_K (earlier run, no p-min) | about 35 | n/a | about 55 |

Run to run noise is about 1 to 3 tokens per second on the end to end numbers (sampling).

Done:
- Each kernel was compared with the existing dp4a kernel for the same layer, on real model tensors, at 1, 2, 4, 7 and 8 columns: normalized MSE about 1e-14 for all six types (differences are float summation order only). This was done with a temporary check inside the dispatch, which is not in the tree.
- test-backend-ops test -o MUL_MAT -b SYCL0: 1132/1132 passed. NOTE: those cases use small `k` (below 1024), where the new kernel declines, so this shows no regression elsewhere but does not exercise the kernel.
- `llama-perplexity` (24 chunks of 512 tokens, text from `docs/`, `-b 32 -ub 32` so the prompt uses the kernel), Q3_K_S: 4.8360 XMX off), 4.8349 (XMX on), 4.8360 (batch 512). Q6_K, Q4_K_S and Q2_K also match within 0.003 (table at the end). Q8_0 not measured.

- Only one GPU model (Arc Pro B70) and one driver. Other Intel GPUs (Xe, Xe2, Arc A-series, Data Center) are untested. `load_2d`, DPAS shapes and the register file sizes are architecture dependent. The 2D block load and DPAS paths are guarded by `__has_include` only, not by a device check.

title: Fix duplicate expert IDs in CUDA mul_mat_id
body: Fixes #24591.`n`nThe CUDA mm_ids_helper counted every expert slot with an ID lower than the current expert when computing the compact offset. If a token selected the same expert more than once, the compact representation still contains one row for that token, so the offset included extra slots and left gaps in ids_src1 and ids_dst. Those gaps could contain uninitialized data and lead to illegal memory access in ggml_mul_mat_id.`n`nCount lower experts once per token instead of once per slot in both the generic and specialized helper paths. This preserves the compact token layout when expert IDs are duplicated.

title: cuda : support required FP32 activations in MUL_MAT_ID
body:
## Overview

Mistral Small 4 requests GGML_PREC_F32 for its expert down-projections because their activations can exceed FP16 range. CUDA currently rejects these MUL_MAT_ID operations, so the scheduler executes them on CPU even when the loader reports all model layers offloaded to GPU.

This change handles that precision requirement through the existing sorted-expert fallback. It keeps the gathered activations in FP32 and calls the existing FP32 cuBLAS implementation for each expert slice.

Fusion paths that cannot preserve this requirement are excluded, and synchronization reporting matches the fallback. Support is limited to NVIDIA devices and the input types and layouts handled by that implementation. HIP and MUSA retain their existing behavior.

The regression tests cover Q4_K, Q8_0 and BF16 weights with activations above FP16 range, including single-token, multi token and fusion graphs. The CUDA operation support table is updated accordingly.

## Additional information

Fixes #30224.

Validation used patched commit 1e29ebb6f358ee40ed15ca0edc32a0af6ea4ee4b against its unpatched parent, 609290be6b15db02f9d73443435403cbff6e7802.

### Correctness

- The focused regression ran on an RTX 3090, RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell and RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell. Before the patch, all 36 selected cases were unsupported. After the patch, all 36 executed and passed against CPU references.
- All 36 cases also passed with `GGML_CUDA_CUBLAS_COMPUTE_TYPE=f16`, confirming that this override does not narrow the required FP32 activations.
- All 18 selected ordinary-operation cases passed.
- Native CPU CI completed: Debug/Release CTest passed 50/50 and 51/51, model-dependent tests passed 5/5 in each build, and 21,885 supported backend-operation cases passed.
- Native CUDA CI on an RTX A5000 completed the same CTest groups and passed 18,515 supported backend-operation cases, including 15 high-amplitude FP32 expert/fusion cases. Unsupported cases are excluded from these pass counts.

The CUDA CI run initially stopped at the final model tests because the temporary environment lacked external GNU `time`. After installing that prerequisite, the two unfinished model-test groups passed using the retained builds.

Real generation with Mistral Small 4 UD-Q4_K_M also succeeded. Scheduler logs placed all 36 expert down-projections on CUDA. The short canary produced the correct arithmetic answer with separate reasoning and final content.

A focused regression selector is:

```sh
./build/bin/test-backend-ops test \
    -b CUDA0 \
    -o MUL_MAT_ID,MUL_MAT_ID_FUSION,MUL_MAT_VEC_FUSION \
    -p 'n_mats=4.*n_used=2.*amax=100000' \
    --output csv
```

### Performance and perplexity

Matched Release builds used GCC 13 and CUDA 13.3.73. The GPU comparison used Ling 3.0 Flash Q4_K_M on the three-GPU configuration above, with unchanged settings and runtime CUDA graphs disabled.

Each benchmark used three repetitions, 512-token prefill and 128-token decode:

| Build | Prefill tok/s, mean ± SD | Decode tok/s, mean ± SD |
|---|---:|---:|
| Baseline before | 714.98 ± 49.87 | 73.16 ± 0.62 |
| Patched | 710.36 ± 70.57 | 73.12 ± 1.15 |
| Baseline after | 719.03 ± 60.68 | 72.87 ± 0.16 |

The patched result differs from the bracketed baseline mean by -0.93% for prefill and +0.14% for decode. This bounded comparison did not demonstrate a meaningful slowdown.

WikiText-2 perplexity, using two 1024-token chunks, was identical at printed precision:

- CUDA, Ling Q4_K_M: `5.2846 ± 0.41607` before and after.
- CPU, the Qwen3 0.6B F16 CI fixture: `9.4179 ± 0.80961` before and after.

CPU benchmarks were also recorded, but the first baseline differed substantially from its repeat. They do not support a claim of a patch-induced CPU speedup.

The patch applied cleanly in memory against upstream commit `10a60cf303566e10d6a7a2774c17d2085503d87b`. That current-master build was not runtime-tested; the results above apply to the tested patch commit.

title: chat : enforce string enums in Qwen XML tool arguments
body:
## Overview

The Qwen XML tool grammar accepts arbitrary strings for a parameter declared as `{"type":"string","enum":["list","load"]}`. For example, `<parameter=action>\nerase\n</parameter>` is accepted even though `erase` is not an allowed value.

The handler selects its unrestricted XML string rule whenever the parameter resolves to a string. It therefore bypasses the JSON converter that would enforce the enum for JSON arguments.

For a nonempty string enum, build the XML value rule from the allowed literal strings instead. Check the closing-parameter boundary when choosing each literal, so an earlier shorter entry does not consume the prefix of a longer one. Ordinary strings and non-string enums retain their existing paths. This patch adds no root-union support, schema adapter, public API, model or GPU change.

## Additional information

### Validation

Rebased September 15 on `54315813269112dd0baed7112ec87ad93a8218ca`; head `a86bd319541a5d0c76cab87c2faadfccd6a16650`. The enum branch uses the current typed schema representation.

Separate matching baseline/candidate Linux x86_64 builds used GCC 15.2, Release, shared libraries, native CPU and OpenMP. All seven selected parser/grammar suites passed on both builds, with zero compiler warnings: `test-chat`, `test-json-schema-to-grammar`, `test-chat-peg-parser`, `test-chat-auto-parser`, `test-chat-template`, `test-grammar-parser` and `test-grammar-integration`.

The exact new `test-chat` binary fails against baseline libraries at the invalid-enum assertion (expected rejection, observed acceptance) and passes against candidate libraries. The added test covers Qwen3-Coder and Qwen3.5 templates, invalid strings, shared-prefix alternatives, empty strings, embedded quotes/newlines, parsed/streamed tool arguments, parallel calls and an unrestricted-string positive control.

This replaces the broader root-union proposal in #28651 following the portability objection there. That representation can be adapted on the client side; ordinary enum enforcement is an independent defect. The same focused fix was submitted first as [Halo staging #26](https://github.com/halo-box/llama.cpp/pull/26).

Not run for this isolated patch: model inference, full CI, other-platform builds, perplexity or performance sweeps. No throughput or general model-quality improvement is claimed.

- This is a human-directed contribution. I own its review follow-up.

title: mtmd: cast the attention mask to f16 once, not once per layer
body:
## What

With flash attention, `clip_graph::build_attn` cast the mask to f16 on every call. A same-type `ggml_cast` is still a full `GGML_OP_CPY`, so:

- `qwen2vl.cpp` already casts its window mask to f16 once, but each of the 28 windowed layers still ran a redundant f16→f16 copy of the whole `n_pos²` mask.
- Models that pass an f32 mask through `build_vit_opts` (`attn_mask` / `attn_mask_layers`) ran one f32→f16 cast per layer.

Two small changes:

1. `build_attn`: only cast when `kq_mask->type != GGML_TYPE_F16`.
2. `build_vit`: cast each distinct mask once before the layer loop (deduplicated by tensor pointer), gated on `flash_attn_type == CLIP_FLASH_ATTN_TYPE_ENABLED`. The non-FA path is unchanged.

## Measured (Vulkan, AMD Radeon 890M / RDNA 3.5, RADV, Mesa 26.2.4)

Qwen2.5-VL-3B (Q4_K_M text, f16 mmproj), 1024×1024 image = 5476 patch tokens, `-ngl 99`, `--temp 0`:

| | CPY ops in encode | CPY time | encode (median of 4, alternating) |
|---|---|---|---|
| master d1d3c339 | 93 | 120 ms | 2648 ms |
| this PR | 65 | 85 ms | 2593 ms |

Generated text is byte-identical. SmolVLM2-2.2B (goes through `build_vit`, no mask) also byte-identical, same encode time.

Not exercised on hardware here: a model that passes a mask via `build_vit_opts` (deepseekocr2, mimo-audio, muse-glimmer). The change there is the same cast, moved earlier.

title: llama : skip logits buffer allocation when graph produces no logits
body:
## Overview

Fixes #29388.

For embedding and reranking models whose compute graph never outputs logits, `output_reserve()` still allocated and zero-filled an `n_vocab * n_outputs` float buffer. For large vocabularies (bge-m3: 250002, EmbeddingGemma: 262144), this wastes roughly 1 MiB host RAM per token. As reported in #29388, at default server concurrency (4 slots sharing up to `n_ubatch` tokens), this caused EmbeddingGemma to get OOM-killed in a 2.6 GB cgroup.

The logits buffer is now kept when embeddings are off, and skipped only when embeddings are on and the reserve graph has no logits tensor.

API change: for models without logits, `llama_get_logits()` returns `NULL` instead of a zero-filled buffer. `llama_get_logits_ith()`  logs an error and triggers  `GGML_ABORT` in Debug builds.

## Additional information

Related:
1.) #29576 touches the same function (sampling buffers) and merges without conflict.
2.) #25964 adds an opt-in flag to skip LM-head compute.

### Memory growth over idle (Q8_0 GGUFs)

`llama-server --embeddings -ub 2048 -b 2048 -np 1 -c 8192 -t 8`

**CPU (`RssAnon` from `/proc/<pid>/status`):**

| Model (vocab) | Prompt tokens (min / max) | master (79e2e74eb) | patched |
|---|---|---|---|
| bge-m3 (250002) | 26 / 1952 | +26 MB / +1939 MB | +1 MB / +81 MB (~1.85 GB saved) |
| EmbeddingGemma-300M (262144) | 18 / 1302 | +19 MB / +1353 MB | +1 MB / +49 MB (~1.3 GB saved) |
| nomic-embed-text-v1.5 (30522) | 18 / 1302 | +5 MB / +238 MB | +3 MB / +77 MB |
| bge-reranker-v2-m3 (rank pooling) | 29 / 1955 | +29 MB / +1943 MB | +1 MB / +81 MB |

**CUDA (`VmRSS` / `RssShmem`, `-ngl 99`):**

On CUDA, the pinned host buffer is accounted for under `RssShmem` rather than `RssAnon`, so `VmRSS` reflects the saving (single request per model):

| Model | Prompt tokens | master (79e2e74eb) | patched |
|---|---|---|---|
| bge-m3 | 1952 | +1878 MB | +17 MB |
| EmbeddingGemma-300M | 1302 | +1315 MB | +13 MB |
| nomic-embed-text-v1.5 | 1302 | +166 MB | +14 MB |

(VRAM usage is unchanged at ~490 MiB on both; the saving is host RAM).

### Testing

Tested on CPU (Intel Xeon Platinum, 8 threads, aws instance: g4dn.2xlarge) and CUDA (Tesla T4, CUDA 13.3, `-ngl 99`). Other backends (Metal, Vulkan, etc.) are untested.

- Parity checks:
  - CPU: embeddings, rerank scores, text generation (stories260K, LFM2, flan-t5-small), and perplexity are bit-identical to master.
  - CUDA: embeddings and rerank scores are identical across all four models; server completions plus embeddings are identical on stories260K and LFM2.
- LFM2 toggle: logits are restored when dynamically switching `llama_set_embeddings()` off (verified on CPU and CUDA).

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES, used ByteAsk agent (with Sonnet)  for A/B benchmark scripts and /proc memory logging. Code changes are minimal and all done by me; results verified by me.

title: server: allow load-on-startup models when --models-max is 0
body:
## Overview

Hello there!   This PR is a very minor change to allow load-on-startup with  --models-max=0.  Huzzah!

Starting the router with `--models-max 0` and a preset that sets `load-on-startup = true` exits during init with `number of models to load on startup (1) exceeds models_max (0)`; this is an inconvenience. 

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->


The README documents `--models-max` as `0 = unlimited`, and the other `models_max` checks in `server-models.cpp` already skip when it is `<= 0`. The startup check was missing that guard; this adds `base_params.models_max > 0 &&` to it, so the behavior here matches the rest of the router.

## Additional information

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

Reproduce this bug with a one-model preset with `load-on-startup = true`, started with `--models-max 0`. On master the server exits 1 before it listens; with this change the model loads.

I added `test_router_load_on_startup_unlimited_models_max` to `tools/server/tests/unit/test_router.py`. It fails on master and passes with the fix; the whole of `test_router.py` passes (18).

Do note, running the new test on its own needs `tools/server/tests/tmp/` to exist. The existing preset tests in that file share the same dependency, so I left that alone.

title: server: allow checkpoint after last media
body:
## Overview

Allow checkpoint to be created after media so change to content after media (message) don't require reprefill of the media content.

## Additional information

Fix for #26994 .
This is easily noticeable when editing message with images in the UI, as the image on the same round get reprefill, even though UI sent image before text.

### To recreate
- Load a hybrid model (Qwen3.5/3.6) or an SWA model (Gemma 3/4) with mmproj.
- Send image + text, then the same image with different text. (with UI just edit the text)
- On the second request the image is reprocessed, see test below.

### Cause & justification
- start with #20232 as a fix for #20222 , #20726 kept the guard in place, with no checkpoint after the media, the only restore point is now before the media.
- Make sense to checkpoint the media tokens as most often it's slow and expensive to reprefill them, at the cost of an extra checkpoint.

## Changes
- is_after_last_media check for first batch follows the last media.
- Relax mid-prompt filter, the guard now only blocks checkpoints between media.

Note: The spacing rule (--checkpoint-min-step) still applies.

## Test
- Add test in test_vision_api.py: tinygemma3 (SWA) and tinyopenjev (hybrid Qwen3.5), assert cached prompt larger than process prompts.

title: CUDA/HIP: matrix-core (MFMA) lightning indexer for CDNA2 (gfx90a)
body:
## Overview

This adds a ROCm matrix-core (MFMA) path for the DeepSeek-V3.2/V4 lightning indexer. The
current non-CUDA path runs the indexer on the scalar `lightning_indexer_kernel_vec`
kernel, which leaves the CDNA matrix cores idle; NVIDIA already has a tensor-core
(`wmma`) path 

The main motivation is DeepSeek-V4 long-context, where the lightning indexer scores every
KV token for top-k sparse-attention selection and its cost grows with context length.

## Performance

Tested with DeepSeek-V4 Flash GGUF (UD-IQ2_XXS, 84.6 GiB) on four MI250X (gfx90a) GCDs
using ROCm 7.2 (`-ngl 99 -fa on -sm layer -b 2048 -ub 512 -r 3`). Back-to-back A/B in the
same window; baseline is the existing `_vec` path (`GGML_INDEXER_NO_MFMA=1`).

title: common : limit the nesting of parsed JSON to 128 levels
body:
## Overview

A request with deeply nested JSON crashes `llama-server` (SIGSEGV on Linux, SIGBUS on macOS). The parse itself is safe, nlohmann parses and frees iteratively, but the parsed tree is then walked with recursion on the HTTP thread: jinja `tojson`, json-schema-to-grammar, `dump()`, the `/v1/systemone` code. httplib worker threads have a 512 KB stack on macOS and 8 MB on Linux.

First depth that crashes the server on master 50e3e3e48 (tested depths 100, 120, 130, 700, 1000, 2000, 10000, 30000, 1000000; LFM2.5-VL-450M for chat, d1-omni-600M for `/v1/systemone`):

| request | macOS, M3 Ultra | Linux x86 |
|---|---|---|
| `/v1/chat/completions`, tool `parameters` schema | 700 | 10,000 |
| `/v1/chat/completions`, `response_format` schema | 700 | 10,000 |
| `/v1/chat/completions`, tool-call `arguments` (object or JSON string) | 2,000 | 30,000 |
| `/v1/systemone`, `state` | 2,000 | 30,000 |

`common_json::parse` now counts the nesting of `[` and `{` outside strings before parsing, and throws `common_json_error` "JSON is nested more than 128 levels deep" above 128 levels; `parse_no_throw` returns a discarded value. All nlohmann parsing goes through these two functions, so the check covers request bodies and the JSON carried in request strings (tool-call `arguments`, `chat_template_kwargs`, `json_schema`). The server answers 400.

## Additional information

Reproduction (crashes at `d=1000` on macOS; use `d=10000` on Linux):

```sh
llama-server -hf LiquidAI/LFM2.5-VL-450M-GGUF:F16 --jinja --port 8080 &
python3 -c "d=1000; s='{\"type\": \"array\", \"items\": '*d+'{\"type\": \"string\"}'+'}'*d; print('{\"messages\": [{\"role\": \"user\", \"content\": \"hi\"}], \"max_tokens\": 1, \"tools\": [{\"type\": \"function\", \"function\": {\"name\": \"f\", \"description\": \"d\", \"parameters\": {\"type\": \"object\", \"properties\": {\"x\": '+s+'}}}}]}')" > deep.json
curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @deep.json
```

With this PR, the same sweep on macOS and Linux: at 100 and 120 levels every request gets the same answer as on master; from 130 to 1,000,000 levels every request gets HTTP 400 and the server stays up. Tool-call `arguments` sent as a JSON string get HTTP 500 instead of 400, because `common/chat.cpp` wraps argument parse errors in `std::runtime_error`, as it already does for malformed arguments.

- 128 is the serde_json default; #29755 proposes 256 for GBNF grammars. The deepest JSON in the repo's tests and fixtures is 7 levels.
- The scan costs 7-33 ms on 7-50 MB bodies, 5-8% of the parse. nlohmann's parser callback has a depth argument, but with `ordered_json` and 200,000 objects it took 21.8 s instead of 0.16 s.
- Regression test: new `depth` group in `test-json-schema` (128 and 129 levels, about 100,000 levels, plain arrays, `parse_no_throw`, an escaped quote before brackets in a string). Without the check, the 100,000-level case crashes the test binary.
- JSON deeper than 128 that does not come from a request is rejected too: an MCP reply is dropped as malformed, an Anthropic `tool_use` input becomes `{}`.

Not fixed here:
- macOS: some chat templates recurse per level in macros and run out of the 512 KB stack below 128 levels (gemma-4 tool-call arguments from 115, gpt-oss tool parameters from 102); with 8 MB they render.
- json-schema-to-grammar recursion that does not come from JSON nesting: long `$ref` chains, a long property name with `additionalProperties`, many optional properties.
- Related: #29690 and #25283 (nested schemas, closed as not planned), #29495 / #29755 (GBNF nesting), #29728 (PEG parser on nested model output, not covered).

## Requirements

- AI usage disclosure: YES, distributed testing and implementation under a human supervision

title: opencl: int8 fused KQ: stage Q per head-size slice and allow head size 512
body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

The fused int8 KQ in the decomposed prefill attention stages the whole Q tile in local memory once per workgroup and keeps all accumulators live through the softmax epilogue, so its local memory grows with the head size and it is limited to head sizes up to 256.

This adds a head-size-512 build of the fused kernel, which stages Q in 256-wide slices per kv block, writes the accumulators to local memory before the epilogue and reuses the Q slice for the scores. Wherever int8 KQ is enabled, f16 KV at head size 512 now takes it for batches of at least 32 queries; narrower verify batches keep the folded f16 KQ. 

Head sizes up to 256 keep the existing kernel, and a head over 256 won't reach the separate int8 KQ.

title: ggml : add FP8 types and CPU conversions
body:
## Overview

This PR adds CPU support for FP8, including the ability to load FP8 weights directly and convert them to FP16, BF16, or FP32.

Many diffusion models already support FP8, and some are even released with FP8 weights natively. On hardware with native FP8 support, FP8 computation can also be faster than FP16/BF16, so having proper FP8 support in GGML would be useful for both model loading and execution.

I'm not sure whether upstream would be happy with this approach, so for now I've only included the CPU-related changes in this PR. If this approach is acceptable, I can follow up with another PR that adds the conversion code for the other backends, as well as FP8 `mul_mat` support for CUDA.

This is the GGML implementation I'm currently using in `sd.cpp`:

* https://github.com/leejet/ggml/commit/e20c3a14aa70ee84ca58499814206dd08d8026bc

For FP8 scale handling, my current idea is to keep the scale as a separate tensor instead of packing it into the FP8 tensor itself. I think this is more flexible and also reduces the maintenance burden.

title: opencl: decode gemma-4 global attention through the FA decomposition at depth
body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

The gemma-4 global attention layers (head size 512, 16 query heads per KV head) decode on the narrow MQ kernel, which splits the 16 heads into subsets that each streams the whole KV range, so at long context those layers read their KV several times per token.

This routes that decode through the existing flash-attention decomposition. Its KQ folds the group's heads into one tile and the direct KQV reads V in the cache's row layout, so K and V are read once per KV head. The decomposition has a fixed per-call cost, so the default covers only the measured shape: X2E, head size 512, GQA >= 16 and n_kv >= 4096. `GGML_OPENCL_FA_DECODE_DECOMPOSE=0` opts out; `=1` forces it for any decode with GQA >= 8.

## Additional information


Depends on #26430 ("opencl: decode and prefill flash attention on Adreno"), which adds the decomposition, the GQA fold, etc.

title: ggml: support non-contiguous SUM (CPU, CUDA, Vulkan)
body:
## Overview

`test-backend-ops` includes `SUM(type=f32,ne=[33,256,1,1],permute=[1,0,2,3])`, which CUDA rejects and which crashes the CPU reference if enabled. Two small changes:
- CUDA: `supports_op` required `ggml_is_contiguous_rows`, but the kernel only requires `ggml_is_contiguously_allocated` (asserted in `ggml_cuda_op_sum` since #10544). The flat CUB reduction is valid for any gap-free view, since summation is order-independent. The `contiguous_rows` check was added in #16559 to keep CI green after that PR introduced permuted SUM test cases, it wasn't based on what the CUDA kernel can actually handle. This change makes `supports_op` match the condition the kernel itself asserts. The kernel is unchanged.
- CPU: `ggml_compute_forward_sum_f32` asserted `nb[0] == sizeof(float)`, so it aborted on non-contiguous rows, reached as soon as the CPU acts as reference (or fallback) for this case. Added a strided path keeping `ggml_float` accumulation; contiguous fast path unchanged. f16/bf16 variants left as-is.
- Vulkan: `supports_op` accepted SUM for any input with contiguous rows, but the kernel sums the tensor as a single flat block, so sliced views returned wrong results. Changed the check to `ggml_is_contiguously_allocated`, matching the CUDA fix (per 0cc4m’s go-ahead).

*Why CPU and CUDA together* : the CPU fix is required for the CUDA case to be testable, since the reference crashes once the case is enabled.

## Additional information

Testing (RTX 3070 Ti Laptop, CUDA 13.3):
- `test-backend-ops -o SUM`: 8/8, permuted case now passing
- Full `test-backend-ops`: 16094/16094
- `perf -o SUM`: unchanged

Ref #14909, #16559.

title: server : escape the special tokens without std::regex
body:
## Overview

A `/v1/systemone` request can crash `llama-server` on Linux when it serves a d1-omni model (reproduced) or a kev model (same code, not run). Both escape `<|name|>` in the request text with `std::regex_replace` and `<\|([A-Za-z0-9_]+)\|>`. libstdc++ matches the name with a recursive call per character, so a `state` of `"<|"` followed by 30,000 letters overflows the 8 MB stack of the HTTP thread. The escape runs while the prompt is built, before any size check. macOS (libc++) is not affected.

This PR replaces the regex with `server_decision_escape_special_tokens()`, a loop that writes the same text (U+00A6 in place of `|` around a `[A-Za-z0-9_]+` name), used by d1-omni (strings and object keys) and kev.

## Additional information

Reproduction (Linux):

```sh
llama-server -hf LiquidAI/d1-omni-600M-GGUF:F16 --port 8080 &
python3 -c "import json; print(json.dumps({'state': '<|' + 'a'*30000, 'questions': {'q': {'type': 'noul', 'instructions': 'Is the text long?'}}}))" > esc.json
curl -s localhost:8080/v1/systemone -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @esc.json
```

Without a model, the regex alone (`g++ -std=c++17 -O2 regex.cpp -o regex && ./regex 20000 && ./regex 30000`):

```cpp
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <regex>
#include <string>
int main(int argc, char ** argv) {
    const std::string s = "<|" + std::string(std::strtoul(argv[1], nullptr, 10), 'a');
    static const std::regex re("<\\|([A-Za-z0-9_]+)\\|>");
    std::printf("%zu\n", std::regex_replace(s, re, "<\xC2\xA6$1\xC2\xA6>").size());
}
```

It crashes between 20,000 and 30,000 characters with the default 8 MB stack; gdb shows 3 frames per character (`_M_dfs` twice, `_M_rep_once_more` once).

Linux x86, master 50e3e3e48 and this PR, d1-omni-600M F16 on the CPU:

| `state` | master | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `"<\|"` + 20,000 letters | HTTP 500 (input too large) | same |
| `"<\|"` + 30,000, 100,000 or 1,000,000 letters | server dies (SIGSEGV) | HTTP 500 (input too large), server up |
| plain text; `<\|...\|>` in the state, keys and options; non-ASCII text | answers | identical answers |

- Same output as the regex: no difference on about 4.5M generated strings (macOS) and on the test's 19,531 strings (Linux). Each input byte is read at most twice.
- Regression test, new `test-server-decision`: fixed cases, every string of up to 6 characters over `<|>a-` against the old regex call, and 1,000,000-character names. With the regex put back, it crashes on Linux.
- A new test file because no C++ test covers `server-decision.cpp`, and the Python tests have no d1-omni or kev model.
- Not fixed here: a deeply nested JSON `state` still crashes the server in jinja `tojson` (about 30,000 levels on Linux); separate PR "common : limit the nesting of parsed JSON to 128 levels".

## Requirements

title: respect -fitc from llama-bench instead of using the benchmark context size
body:
## Overview

While tweaking the optimal settings for running Qwen 3.6 MoE on a small mobile GPU plus System RAM, I was wondering why what `llama-fit-params` used with `llama-bench` produced different results that using `-fitc` with llama-bench directly.

*Disclosure:* I used AI (Qwen 3.6, of course via llama-server) for the analysis and the fix. These words here are my own though.

## Additional information

Turns out that llama-bench does not use my `-fitc 196608` parameter (I wanted to benchmark for) for fitting, but strictly the actual benchmark context size (pp512 plus tg128, makes only 640 tokens). All that `-fitc` does is enable fitting.
I then tried absurdly different `-fitc 16384` as well as `-fitc 1638400` parameters to verify, and all produced the same benchmark result (higher, as more layers and parameters fit on the GPU).

At the changed code, if `n_ctx_auto` is false (which is always the case with llama-bench), it now clamps the context size for fit calculation to the passed `-fitc` parameter via `fit_min_ctx` if it is bigger (most likely in practice) than the benchmark's token requirements.

This way the benchmark runs with the same settings I get from `llama-fit-params` with the actual context I plan to run llama-server with.

title: ggml: fix OOB write in ggml_acc / ggml_set with negative offset
body:
## Overview

  ggml_acc and ggml_set read the op offset from op_params[3] into a size_t.
  op_params[3] is an int32_t. A negative value sign-extends to a huge size_t.
  The existing bounds assertion then wraps around and passes. The write lands
  before the dst buffer. This is an out-of-bounds write.

  The fix reads the offset as int32_t, asserts it is non-negative, then casts
  it to size_t. This applies to acc_f32, set_f32 and set_i32.

  ## Additional information

  The negative offset can come from the size_t to int32_t narrowing in
  ggml_acc_impl and ggml_set_impl, or from the RPC GRAPH_COMPUTE path that
  copies op_params from the wire without validation.

  An ASan build reports heap-buffer-overflow (WRITE/READ of size 4) four bytes
  before the dst buffer when the forward runs with op_params[3] = -4. With this
  patch, the same input trips the GGML_ASSERT instead.

  ## Requirements

title: model : use exact GELU for ModernBERT encoders
body:
## Overview

ModernBERT models with `hidden_activation: "gelu"` currently run the tanh approximation through `ggml_geglu`, but transformers uses exact GELU. This switches `gelu`, and the default when the key is missing, to `ggml_geglu_erf`.

Names that mean the tanh approximation (`gelu_pytorch_tanh`, `gelu_new`, `gelu_fast`, `gelu_accurate`, `gelu_python_tanh`) stay on `ggml_geglu`, and SiLU models are unchanged. Existing GGUFs work without reconversion.

Follow-up to #29692, where @CISC pointed out that transformers `gelu` is exact GELU, not the tanh approximation. That PR fixed the rank head, and the encoder FFN had the same mismatch.

## Additional information

Tested on CPU in F32 with `Alibaba-NLP/gte-reranker-modernbert-base`, comparing against transformers on 24 query/passage pairs:

| | master | PR |
|---|---|---|
| FFN activation, max error vs exact GELU | 5.8e-2 | 7.4e-6 |
| encoder output, mean error vs transformers | 3.5e-4 | 1.3e-4 |
| encoder output, max error vs transformers | 7.2e-3 | 2.8e-3 |

The tanh variants and SiLU (`ibm-granite/granite-embedding-97m-multilingual-r2`) give byte-identical outputs before and after.

The remaining difference comes from the F16 cast of K and V before flash attention in `build_attn_mha`. With `-fa off`, scores match transformers to 1e-6 (max 5.7e-6), and every layer matches to about 1e-6, including the sliding window layers on a 411 token input.

On CPU the speed change was within run-to-run noise; the SiLU model, which this change doesn't touch, varied by up to 18% between runs. GPU not tested.

Build with fatal warnings, ctest `main|python`, server embedding and rerank tests, and `test-llama-archs` all pass.
